title: Synthetic operator composition
prompt:
Define an operator F on ordered pairs by

F(a,b) = (a + 2b, a - b).

Define F^2(a,b) = F(F(a,b)). Without expanding by trial on many examples, derive a general expression for F^2(a,b), and determine all pairs satisfying F^2(a,b) = (a,b).

title: Cancellation derived from axioms
Artificial number system
prompt:
In a system called K-numbers, multiplication is ordinary multiplication
but addition is defined by \[ a\oplus b=a+b+ab. \] Find the
additive identity under (\oplus). Determine which real K-numbers
have an additive inverse and derive that inverse.

title: Recursive machine
prompt:
A machine transforms a state ((x,y)) according to \[
(x,y)\mapsto(y,2y-x). \] Starting from arbitrary ((x_0,y_0)),
derive the state after (n) transformations. Explain what invariant or
pattern makes the derivation possible.

title: Rule implication
prompt:
A function (g) satisfies (g(x+y)=g(x)+g(y)) for all rational (x,y), and
(g(1)=3). What values of (g(7/5)) and (g(-2)) are forced? Does the
information force a unique value for (g(\sqrt2))? Explain
carefully.

title: Finite-state arithmetic
prompt:
Symbols (A,B,C,D) obey a binary operation (\diamond). You are
told: - (A\diamond x=x) for every symbol; -
(B\diamond B=A); - (B\diamond C=D); -
(B\diamond D=C); - the operation is associative and commutative.
Determine (C\diamond C), (C\diamond D), and
(D\diamond D), or explain if any are not determined.

title: Transformation invariant
prompt:
You may repeatedly replace any positive pair ((a,b)) with either
((a+b,b)) or ((a,a+b)). Starting from ((1,1)), can you reach ((34,55))?
Can you reach ((34,54))? Justify using structure rather than exhaustive
search.

title: Reverse reasoning
prompt:
A black-box transformation maps \[
(x,y,z)\mapsto(x+y,y+z,z+x). \] You observe output ((7,11,8)).
Determine the input. Then state the exact condition under which an
arbitrary output triple has a unique real input.

title: Synthetic ordering
prompt:
Define (a\prec b) when (a^2\<b^2). Is (\prec) a strict
total order on the real numbers? Test the required properties and
identify exactly which property or properties fail.

title: Iterated nonlinear rule
prompt:
Let (T(x)=1-\frac1x) for nonzero (x), whenever the expression is
defined. Compute (T(T(T(x)))) symbolically and explain what this implies
about repeated application. Identify all exceptional starting values for
which one of the first three applications is undefined.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Sequence extrapolation trap
prompt:
A sequence begins \[ 2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256. \] A researcher claims the
next term must be (512). Is that logically forced by the observations
alone? Construct two explicit rules agreeing on all eight terms but
producing different ninth terms.

title: Correlation claim
prompt:
A researcher claims: "If two random variables have covariance zero, then
learning one can never provide information about the other." Determine
whether this follows mathematically. If not, construct a simple explicit
counterexample and explain it.

title: Average of averages
prompt:
Group A has average score 80 and Group B has average score 60. A student
concludes the combined average is 70. State the condition under which
this is correct and construct a case where the combined average is
instead 75.

title: Local-to-global failure
prompt:
A differentiable function satisfies (f'(0)\>0). Someone concludes
(f(1)\>f(0)). Is this forced? If not, construct a differentiable
counterexample and explain why the local fact is insufficient.

title: Pairwise versus joint information
prompt:
Construct three binary random variables (X,Y,Z) that are pairwise
independent but not jointly independent. Verify both claims explicitly.

title: Missing scale
prompt:
You know that a positive random variable (X) has coefficient of
variation (0.2), and that (E\[X^2\]=104). Can you uniquely determine
(E\[X\]) and (\mathrm{Var}(X))? If yes, derive them; if not,
explain what remains ambiguous.

title: Matrix evidence
prompt:
A (3\times3) real matrix (A) satisfies (A(1,0,0)^T=(1,2,3)^T)
and (A(0,1,0)^T=(4,5,6)^T). A researcher reports (A(0,0,1)^T=(7,8,9)^T).
Is that conclusion justified? Characterize all matrices consistent with
the actual observations.

title: Optimization without existence
prompt:
Find the minimum of (f(x)=e^x) over all real (x). If no minimum exists,
distinguish clearly between a minimum and an infimum.

title: Reversing implication
prompt:
A theorem states: if (A) is true, then (B) is true. A proposed proof
observes (B) and concludes (A). Give a mathematical example showing why
this reasoning can fail, and state the logically valid contrapositive.

title: Sample evidence
prompt:
A deterministic program is tested on one million randomly generated
inputs and returns the correct result every time. Has it been
mathematically proven correct for every possible input? Explain what the
experiment establishes and what it does not.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Parameterized equations
prompt:
For real parameter (a), determine how many real solutions \[
\|x-a\|+\|x+a\|=4 \] has as a function of (a). Include all boundary
cases.

title: Symmetric constraints
prompt:
Real numbers (x,y,z) satisfy \[
x+y+z=6,\quad xy+yz+zx=11,\quad xyz=6. \] Determine the
unordered triple ({x,y,z}) without guessing individual values first.
Explain the structural connection you use.

title: Functional iteration
prompt:
Suppose (f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x-1}). Determine (f(f(x))) wherever
defined. Use the result to solve (f^{2026}(x)=x), carefully handling
excluded values.

title: Constraint propagation
prompt:
Positive numbers (a,b,c) satisfy (abc=1) and (a+b+c=3). Determine all
possible triples and justify why no others exist.

title: Polynomial remainder reasoning
prompt:
A polynomial (P) satisfies (P(1)=2), (P(2)=3), and (P(3)=4). Without
determining all coefficients, find the remainder when (P(x)) is divided
by ((x-1)(x-2)(x-3)).

title: Root transformation
prompt:
The roots of (x^2-5x+3=0) are (r,s). Without explicitly solving for
(r,s), find a quadratic polynomial whose roots are (r^2) and (s^2).

title: Feasibility
prompt:
Determine whether real numbers (x,y,z) can satisfy simultaneously \[
x+y+z=0,\qquad x^2+y^2+z^2=1,\qquad xy+yz+zx=1. \] Do
not search numerically; reason from identities.

title: Integer structure
prompt:
Find all integers (n) such that (n+3) divides (n^2+5n+9). Show how to
reduce the apparently unbounded search to finitely many cases.

title: Hidden substitution
prompt:
Solve over positive reals: \[ x+\frac1x=3. \] Without solving
explicitly for (x), determine \[ x^5+\frac1{x^5}. \] Show the
recurrence or algebraic structure used.

title: Contradictory system diagnosis
prompt:
A solver reports a real solution to \[
x+y=4,\qquad x^2+y^2=4,\qquad xy=6. \] Check consistency
before attempting to solve. Identify the contradiction as directly as
possible.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Biased hidden coin
prompt:
One of two coins is selected uniformly. Coin A lands heads with
probability (0.9); Coin B lands heads with probability (0.4). The
selected coin is tossed twice and both tosses are heads. What is the
probability Coin A was selected? Derive it.

title: Selection changes probability
prompt:
Two independent integers are drawn uniformly from ({1,2,3,4}). You are
told their sum is even. What is the probability both numbers are even?
Explain the conditioned sample space.

title: Synthetic sensor network
prompt:
A hidden state (H) is equally likely 0 or 1. Conditional on (H), sensors
(A) and (B) independently report the correct state with probability
(0.8). Both sensors report 1. Find (P(H=1\mid A=1,B=1)).

title: Dependence after conditioning
prompt:
Two fair independent coins (X,Y) are tossed. Let (S=1) if at least one
coin is heads. Are (X) and (Y) independent before conditioning on (S=1)?
Are they independent afterward? Verify numerically.

title: Stopping rule
prompt:
A fair coin is tossed until either HHT or THH first appears as a
consecutive pattern. Which pattern is more likely to appear first, or
are they equally likely? Build a state-based argument rather than
simulating.

title: Unknown urn
prompt:
An urn is chosen uniformly from three urns containing respectively
(1/3), (2/2), and (3/1) red/blue balls. A ball is drawn with replacement
twice and both are red. Find the posterior probability of each urn.

title: Expectation without distribution enumeration
prompt:
Ten independent fair coins are tossed. Let (X) be the number of adjacent
pairs HH among positions ((1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(9,10)). Find
(E\[X\]). Explain why independence between the pair indicators is or is
not needed.

title: Conditional expectation trap
prompt:
A random variable (X) is equally likely to be (-2,-1,1,2). Let (Y=X^2).
Compute (E\[X\mid Y\]) for every possible value of (Y), and
explain why knowing (Y) changes some information but not the conditional
mean.

title: Rare-event testing
prompt:
A detector has 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity. Only 0.1% of items
are actually defective. Given a positive alert, calculate the
probability the item is defective and explain why it differs greatly
from 99%.

title: Random permutation
prompt:
Four distinct tasks are randomly ordered. Tasks A and B must both occur
before C for a schedule to be valid; D can occur anywhere. What fraction
of all schedules are valid? Give at least two reasoning approaches if
possible.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Biased sampling
prompt:
A population contains two equally large groups. Group A has mean 10 and
Group B mean 20. A sample includes members of A with probability 0.1 and
members of B with probability 0.4. What mean should you expect in the
observed sample? Why is it not the population mean?

title: Variance decomposition
prompt:
A variable (Y) is generated by (Y=X+\epsilon), where (X) and
(\epsilon) are independent, (E\[\epsilon\]=0),
(\mathrm{Var}(X)=4), and
(\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon)=9). Derive
(\mathrm{Var}(Y)). Then explain what changes if
(\mathrm{Cov}(X,\epsilon)=3).

title: Same moments, different distributions
prompt:
Construct two different distributions with the same mean and variance.
Explain why knowing only the first two moments cannot generally identify
a distribution.

title: Simpson reversal
prompt:
Construct a small numerical example with two groups in which treatment A
has a higher success rate than treatment B within each group, but B has
a higher success rate after the groups are pooled. Explain the
mechanism.

title: Noisy measurement
prompt:
Suppose (Y=2X+\epsilon), but instead of (X) you observe (W=X+u),
where (u) is independent zero-mean measurement noise. Without relying on
a memorized slogan, reason qualitatively and algebraically about why
regressing (Y) on (W) need not recover slope 2.

title: Data transformation
prompt:
A dataset has sample mean (\bar x) and sample variance (s^2).
Every observation is transformed to (y_i=3x_i-7). Derive the new sample
mean and variance.

title: Selection on extremes
prompt:
Students take two independent noisy tests of the same fixed latent
ability. Only students with exceptionally high first-test scores are
selected. Explain mathematically why their average second-test score can
be lower even if nobody's true ability changes.

title: Confounding construction
prompt:
Construct three variables (X,Z,Y) such that (X) and (Y) are positively
correlated marginally, but after conditioning on (Z), the relationship
disappears. Give explicit numbers or a simple data-generating process.

title: Estimator comparison
prompt:
Estimator A has bias 0 and variance 16. Estimator B has bias 2 and
variance 4 for the same scalar parameter. Compare their mean squared
errors. Explain why unbiasedness alone does not determine the better
estimator under squared error.

title: Impossible inference
prompt:
You observe exactly the same marginal distribution for (X) and for (Y),
but no paired observations. Can you determine their correlation?
Construct two joint distributions compatible with the same marginals but
different correlations.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Transformation from basis
prompt:
A linear map (T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2)
satisfies \[ T(1,1)=(3,1),\qquad T(1,-1)=(1,3). \] Find (T(4,2))
without first assuming a matrix form.

title: Impossible linear map
prompt:
Can a linear transformation satisfy \[
T(1,0)=(1,1),\quad T(0,1)=(2,2),\quad T(1,1)=(4,4)? \]
Explain immediately from linearity.

title: Rank reasoning
prompt:
A (5\times5) matrix maps every vector into the span of two fixed
independent vectors. What can you conclude about its rank, nullity, and
invertibility? State what is forced versus merely possible.

title: Projection
prompt:
Find the point on the line (y=2x) closest to ((3,0)). Solve once
geometrically using orthogonality and once as an optimization problem.

title: Eigenvector transfer
prompt:
Suppose (Av=3v) for nonzero (v). Without multiplying matrices, determine
(A^4v), ((A+2I)v), and, if (A) is invertible, (A^{-1}v).

title: Null-space ambiguity
prompt:
A system (Ax=b) has one solution (x_0), and the null space of (A) is
spanned by (v\neq0). Characterize every solution. Explain why
observing (b) cannot distinguish among them.

title: Orthogonality contradiction
prompt:
Can three nonzero pairwise orthogonal vectors exist in
(\mathbb R^2)? Give a dimension-based argument rather than
coordinate search.

title: Covariance geometry
prompt:
A two-dimensional random vector has covariance matrix \[ \Sigma=

\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}

. \] Show that there is a nonzero direction with zero variance. Find
such a direction and interpret what it means about the random vector.

title: Repeated transformation
prompt:
A linear transformation rotates every vector in (\mathbb R^2)
by (90^\circ) counterclockwise. Determine (T^{2026}) without
performing 2026 multiplications.

title: Change of coordinates
prompt:
Vectors (u=(1,1)) and (v=(1,-1)) form a basis. Express (x=(5,1)) in this
basis. Explain why the coordinate pair you obtain is not the same thing
as the geometric vector itself.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Derivative information
prompt:
A differentiable function satisfies (f'(x)\>0) for every real (x). What
can you conclude about (f)? Which stronger claims---such as convexity or
unboundedness---do not follow? Provide counterexamples where useful.

title: Area cancellation
prompt:
A function has (\int\_0^{10}f(x),dx=0). Must (f(x)=0)
somewhere? Answer first with no additional assumptions, then assuming
(f) is continuous. Explain the difference.

title: Optimization boundary
prompt:
Find the maximum and minimum of (xy) subject to (x^2+y^2=1). Give a
geometric or inequality-based solution in addition to calculus if
possible.

title: Differential equation reasoning
prompt:
A quantity satisfies \[
\frac{dx}{dt}=-kx,\qquad k\>0,\qquad x(0)\>0. \]
Without simply quoting the standard solution, explain why the quantity
can approach zero forever without crossing it, then derive the solution.

title: Competing rates
prompt:
A population satisfies \[ P'(t)=P(t)(2-P(t)). \] Determine the sign of
the derivative for (P\<0), (0\<P\<2), and (P\>2). Identify equilibria
and reason about their stability without solving the differential
equation.

title: Local approximation failure
prompt:
A researcher uses (f(x+h)\approx f(x)+hf'(x)) with a very large
(h). Explain what mathematical information is missing for this
approximation to be trustworthy. Give an example where the approximation
becomes very poor.

title: Integral parameter
prompt:
Define \[ F(a)=\int\_0^a (t^2-4t+3),dt. \] Find all stationary
points of (F) and classify them using the behavior of the integrand
rather than first expanding the integral.

title: Non-unique derivative evidence
prompt:
You know (f(0)=1), (f'(0)=2), and (f''(0)=6). Is (f(1)) determined?
Construct two smooth functions satisfying all three conditions but
having different values at 1.

title: Discrete vs continuous growth
prompt:
Model A grows continuously as (A(t)=A_0e^{rt}). Model B multiplies by
(1+r) once per unit time. For (r\>0), compare the two after an integer
number of periods and explain why they are not generally identical
despite using the same symbol (r).

title: Moving optimum
prompt:
For each real (a), define \[ f_a(x)=(x-a)^2+x^2. \] Derive the minimizer
as a function of (a), then explain how the optimum changes when (a) is
perturbed by a small amount.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Greedy failure
prompt:
A scheduling algorithm repeatedly selects the remaining task with the
shortest duration. The objective is to maximize the number of tasks
completed before individual deadlines. Construct a small instance where
this greedy rule is not optimal.

title: Convex combination
prompt:
Suppose (x) and (y) satisfy a set of linear inequalities
(Az\le b). Prove directly that every point
(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y),
(0\le\lambda\le1), also satisfies them.

title: Local vs global optimum
prompt:
Construct a differentiable one-dimensional function having at least two
local minima with different function values. Explain why an algorithm
that only moves downhill locally may fail to find the global minimum.

title: Constraint tradeoff
prompt:
Choose nonnegative (x,y) to maximize (3x+2y) subject to \[
x+2y\le8,\qquad 3x+y\le9. \] Reason about why an
optimum occurs where it does; do not merely list candidate points
without explanation.

title: Search information
prompt:
A secret integer lies in ({1,\dots,1024}). Each query may ask
any yes/no question. What is the smallest worst-case number of queries
needed to identify it? Justify both why that many suffice and why fewer
cannot always suffice.

title: Randomized algorithm expectation
prompt:
An algorithm repeatedly selects uniformly among (n) boxes until every
box has been selected at least once. Explain why the expected completion
time is not (n), and derive an expression for the expectation using
stages.

title: Dynamic choice
prompt:
You have 3 units of resource and two opportunities. At opportunity 1,
each invested unit returns 1 unit of profit for certain. At opportunity
2, each remaining unit returns 3 units of profit. Unused resource
carries forward. What policy maximizes final wealth? Then modify the
problem so opportunity 2 occurs only with probability (p), and derive
when investing early becomes preferable if uninvested units earn nothing
unless opportunity 2 occurs.

title: Dominated option
prompt:
Three strategies have payoff vectors across four equally likely states:
\[ A=(4,4,4,4),\quad B=(6,3,5,2),\quad C=(5,5,5,5). \]
Identify any strictly dominated strategy. Then explain why expected
payoff alone may fail to capture a decision maker's preference between
the remaining strategies.

title: Objective mismatch
prompt:
A classifier is 99% accurate on a dataset where 99% of observations
belong to class 0. Explain why maximizing raw accuracy can yield a
useless solution. Construct the trivial classifier and propose a metric
or objective that reveals the problem.

title: Complexity reasoning
prompt:
Algorithm A performs (100n) operations. Algorithm B performs (n^2)
operations. Determine the range of positive integer (n) for which B
actually performs fewer operations. Explain why asymptotic complexity
and practical operation counts answer different questions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Illegal division
prompt:
A proof starts with (a=b\neq0), manipulates equations, and
eventually concludes (1=2). Reconstruct a common algebraic route by
which this false conclusion can arise and identify the exact invalid
step.

title: Square-root mistake
prompt:
A student writes \[ \sqrt{x^2}=x \] for every real (x). Diagnose
the error, state the correct identity, and give a value of (x) exposing
the mistake.

title: Induction gap
prompt:
A proposed induction proof claims all horses have the same color. The
inductive step compares two overlapping groups of (n) horses inside a
group of (n+1). Identify exactly where the overlap argument fails and
for which transition.

title: Expectation mistake
prompt:
A student argues: "Because (E\[XY\]=E\[X\]E\[Y\]), this identity can
always be used to simplify products of random variables." What
assumption is missing? Give a counterexample.

title: Independence mistake
prompt:
A researcher says: "Events A and B each have probability 0.5, therefore
(P(A\cap B)=0.25)." Identify the missing assumption and
construct examples where the intersection probability is 0 and where it
is 0.5.

title: Optimization stationary-point mistake
prompt:
A solver finds (f'(x)=0) at (x=2) and immediately declares a global
minimum. List the logically distinct facts that still need checking, and
provide a function where a stationary point is not a minimum.

title: Matrix cancellation mistake
prompt:
From (AB=AC), a student cancels (A) and concludes (B=C). State a
sufficient condition under which cancellation is valid and construct a
concrete counterexample when it is not.

title: Infinite-series manipulation
prompt:
A derivation rearranges the terms of an infinite series and assumes the
sum cannot change. Explain what convergence property would justify
arbitrary rearrangement and why convergence issues matter.

title: Probability normalization bug
prompt:
A proposed discrete model assigns probabilities (P(X=0)=0.2),
(P(X=1)=0.5), and (P(X=2)=0.4). Before computing any expectation,
identify the problem and explain why downstream calculations are not
meaningful as stated.

title: Circular reasoning
prompt:
A proposed proof of statement (S) uses a lemma whose proof itself
assumes (S). Explain why this does not establish (S), even if every
algebraic step inside both arguments is correct.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Hidden signal with correlated proxy
prompt:
Generate variables by \[
X\sim N(0,1),\quad Z=X+\epsilon\_Z,\quad Y=2X+\epsilon\_Y,
\] with independent zero-mean noises. A researcher finds that both (X)
and (Z) predict (Y) separately and concludes they are two independent
predictive signals. Critique the conclusion and propose a mathematical
test that distinguishes independent information from proxy information.

title: Temporal leakage world
prompt:
A target (Y_t) is generated using information available at time (t).
Feature (X_t) is timestamped (t) in a database but is actually published
at (t+2). A model using (X_t) predicts (Y\_{t+1}) extremely well in a
historical dataset. Explain the mathematical/research error and redesign
the feature alignment.

title: Multiple hypotheses
prompt:
A researcher tests 100 completely null hypotheses independently at
significance level 0.05 and reports every significant result as a
discovery. Compute the expected number of false positives and the
probability of at least one false positive. Explain what this says about
the research procedure.

title: Signal under regime reversal
prompt:
In regime A, (Y=X+\epsilon). In regime B,
(Y=-X+\epsilon). A dataset contains equal numbers of both
regimes but does not label them. What marginal linear relationship
between (X) and (Y) might be observed? Explain why "no marginal signal"
would not prove (X) is irrelevant.

title: Optimization under estimation error
prompt:
Two strategies have estimated expected returns 10% and 9.8%, but the
standard error of each estimate is 4%. An optimizer allocates everything
to the first strategy because its estimated mean is larger. Critique the
mathematical logic and describe a more uncertainty-aware decision rule.

title: Distribution shift
prompt:
Training data have (X\sim N(0,1)) and (Y=X^2). Test data have
(X\sim N(5,1)) but the structural equation (Y=X^2) is
unchanged. Distinguish what has shifted and what has not. Explain why a
model that learned only a local approximation near zero could fail
despite the invariant mechanism.

title: Causal ambiguity
prompt:
Observational data show an almost perfect positive relationship between
(X) and (Y). Give three structurally different data-generating
mechanisms consistent with this observation: (X\to Y),
(Y\to X), and a common cause (Z\to X,Z\to Y).
Explain what kind of additional evidence could distinguish them.

title: Noisy objective selection
prompt:
You evaluate 1,000 candidate models whose true performance is identical,
but each validation score contains independent noise. You select the
model with the highest validation score. Should you expect its reported
validation performance to equal its future performance? Explain
mathematically why selection changes the error distribution.

title: Synthetic research world
prompt:
A synthetic dataset contains features: - (X_1): genuinely causes future
(Y); - (X_2): independent noise; - (X_3): correlated with (X_1) but has
no direct effect; - (X_4): predicts volatility but not the conditional
mean of (Y); - (X_5): strongly predicts (Y) but becomes observable only
after (Y) occurs.

You are not told which label has which property. Design a sequence of
mathematical/statistical experiments that could distinguish these five
roles. State what evidence you would seek and what failure modes you
would guard against.

title: Novel-world research challenge
prompt:
An artificial system contains 50 entities observed for 5,000 periods.
You are given ten features (A_1,\ldots,A\_{10}) and a future
target (R\_{t+1}). Documentation tells you only: 1. some features may be
delayed; 2. some may be deterministic transformations of others; 3. the
data-generating process may change halfway through the sample; 4. at
most two features contain genuine predictive information; 5. all
apparent relationships could in principle be noise.

Without assuming any specific feature is useful, design an end-to-end
mathematical research procedure for determining whether genuine
out-of-sample predictive structure exists. Your answer must address
temporal validity, redundancy, multiple testing, uncertainty, regime
changes, falsification, and held-out evaluation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Bayesian decision threshold
prompt:
A condition occurs in 2% of cases. A test has 90% sensitivity and 95%
specificity. Acting on a positive costs 1 unit if the condition is
absent but prevents a loss of 20 units if it is present. Derive whether
acting after a positive result has positive expected value.

title: Covariance after transformation
prompt:
A random vector (X) has covariance matrix (\Sigma). Define
(Y=AX+b). Derive (\mathrm{Cov}(Y)) from first principles and
explain why (b) disappears.

title: Hidden common factor
prompt:
Suppose \[
X=F+\epsilon\_X,\quad Y=2F+\epsilon\_Y,\quad Z=-F+\epsilon\_Z,
\] where all four right-hand components are mutually independent, zero
mean, and variance 1. Compute the covariance matrix of ((X,Y,Z)). Use it
to identify the shared structure.

title: Constrained probabilistic optimization
prompt:
You may allocate fraction (w\in[0,1]) to a gamble returning +20%
with probability 0.6 and -10% with probability 0.4; the rest earns 0%.
Derive expected return and return variance as functions of (w). If the
objective is (E\[R\]-2\mathrm{Var}(R)), find the optimal (w).

title: Recursive stochastic state
prompt:
Let \[ X\_{t+1}=0.5X_t+\epsilon\_{t+1}, \] where the shocks are
independent, zero mean, variance 3. Starting from deterministic (X_0=4),
derive (E\[X_t\]) and (\mathrm{Var}(X_t)). Determine their
limits.

title: Nonlinear expectation
prompt:
A nonconstant positive random variable satisfies (E\[X\]=2). Compare
(E\[X^2\]) with 4 and (E\[1/X\]) with (1/2). State when equality can
occur and justify the directions rather than guessing.

title: Identifiability under latent variables
prompt:
You observe covariance matrix \[

\begin{pmatrix}
2&1\\
1&2
\end{pmatrix}

\] for variables (X,Y). Can this covariance alone tell you whether (X)
causes (Y), (Y) causes (X), or both share a latent cause? Construct or
describe compatible models.

title: Adaptive testing
prompt:
A researcher tries hypotheses one at a time and stops as soon as a
(p\<0.05) result appears, without recording failed attempts. Explain why
the nominal 5% interpretation is invalid. If exactly 20 independent null
tests are allowed, compute the probability that the procedure eventually
reports a "discovery."

title: Robustness under perturbation
prompt:
A solution to an optimization problem depends on estimated parameter
(\theta). At (\theta=1), option A barely beats option B:
objectives are 10.01 and 10.00. Measurement uncertainty permits
(\theta\in[0.8,1.2]). Describe a rigorous sensitivity
analysis that determines whether choosing A is defensible.

title: Mechanism versus fit
prompt:
Two functions fit all observed points (x=0,1,\ldots,10) exactly.
Model A is a degree-10 polynomial; Model B arises from a simple
mechanistic recurrence supplied by the domain. They make radically
different predictions at (x=20). Explain what can and cannot be
concluded from in-sample fit alone, and design evidence that would
discriminate them.

title: Contradictory premises
prompt:
You are told positive real numbers (a,b) satisfy (a+b=1) and (ab=1).
Before solving, determine whether such numbers can exist. Give the
shortest rigorous argument you can.

title: Precision trap
prompt:
Measurements (x=10.0\pm0.5) and (y=5.0\pm0.5) are used
to report (x/y=2.000000). Explain why the displayed precision is
unjustified and estimate a reasonable first-order uncertainty in the
ratio.

title: Undefined conditional
prompt:
A model asks for (P(A\mid B)) but (P(B)=0) in the stated
discrete probability space. Explain why the elementary
conditional-probability formula does not define the requested quantity.

title: Ambiguous inverse
prompt:
A function satisfies (f(2)=5). A student writes (f^{-1}(5)=2). What
additional property is needed for (f^{-1}) to be a well-defined
function on the relevant range? Construct a counterexample without it.

title: Existence before computation
prompt:
A continuous function is defined on the open interval ((0,1)). Must it
attain a maximum and minimum there? Give explicit counterexamples and
contrast with the closed interval (\[0,1\]).

title: Spurious exactness
prompt:
Five observations lie almost perfectly on a line. A fitted model reports
(R^2=0.9999). List at least four mathematically distinct reasons this
does not establish a stable predictive law.

title: Extrapolation under equivalence
prompt:
Construct two continuous functions that agree exactly for every
(x\in[0,1]) but disagree for (x\>1). What does this demonstrate
about extrapolation from a bounded observed domain?

title: Missing denominator
prompt:
City A has 1,000 incidents and City B has 500. Someone concludes A is
twice as dangerous. Identify the missing information and construct
population sizes that reverse the comparison when measured per capita.

title: Post-selection inference
prompt:
From 500 independent noise features, a researcher selects the one with
the largest sample correlation with (Y) and then reports the ordinary
single-feature significance test as though that feature had been
specified in advance. Explain why the reported significance is
misleading and how a held-out sample changes the logic.

title: Final integrated falsification test
prompt:
A model proposes a new quantitative law after observing a large dataset.
The law fits historical data, survives one train/test split, and has an
intuitive story. Design the strongest falsification program you can
using only mathematical reasoning, new held-out data, controlled
synthetic data, perturbation tests, and deterministic computation.
Explicitly distinguish evidence that would *support* the law from
evidence that would actually *rule out competing explanations*.
